summary: Draft Session Manager Kernel record. `GlobalTimerResolutionRequests` sits under `HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Session Manager\\Kernel`, has an explicit repo-doc default of `0`, is absent on the observed clean baseline, produced an exact current-build Unicode string hit in `ntoskrnl.exe`, and was later carried forward by source-enrichment as a docs-first current-build kernel candidate with a `power-request-simulation` trigger recommendation. A later KVM local-KD pass then showed the live current-build global `KiGlobalTimerResolutionRequests = 0`, aligning the running kernel with the repo-doc default. The broad lightweight runtime batch then wrote the candidate value as `1` and still returned `no-hit`, while a later repo-native follow-up added an explicit `power-request-simulation` harness to both the generic Procmon guest tool and the mega-trigger runtime surface. The lane is strong enough for a schema-backed draft, but still lacks an exact runtime registry read and a current-build reader or seeding path.

setting.name: Global Timer Resolution Requests
setting.casual_explanation: This appears to be a kernel-level Session Manager setting tied to how the kernel handles global timer-resolution requests. It is kernel-adjacent and is being tracked as a research candidate, not a user-facing tweak.
setting.why_people_change_it: Kernel researchers may inspect this value when investigating timer-resolution behavior, power-request interactions, or undocumented timer-policy tuning.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: The value now has a stronger docs-first evidence chain because it has repo docs, baseline state, exact current-build string presence, a live current-build KD value that matches the repo-doc default, a repo-native `power-request-simulation` harness, and a real write-and-reboot runtime lane. It is still too weak for a published tweak because the exact current-build reader path, any persisted seeding path, and an exact runtime registry read remain unresolved.
setting.professional_notes: Repo docs assign `GlobalTimerResolutionRequests = 0` under `Session Manager\\Kernel` and map it to `KiGlobalTimerResolutionRequests`. The observed clean baseline later confirmed that the parent key exists while the value itself is absent. The broad current-build string batch found an exact Unicode hit for `GlobalTimerResolutionRequests` in `ntoskrnl.exe`. Later source-enrichment kept the candidate in the canonical queue with the same docs-first route bucket and, unlike many raw docs-only leads, converged on a concrete low-priority trigger family: `power-request-simulation`, with suggested primitives such as `PowerCreateRequest(SystemRequired)`, `PowerSetRequest(DisplayRequired)`, and an audio playback session. A later KVM local-KD pass then resolved `nt!KiGlobalTimerResolutionRequests` in the live current-build kernel and returned `0`, which matches the repo-doc default and removes the older live-state gap. The broad tools-hardened lightweight runtime lane still wrote all 21 `Session Manager\\Kernel` batch values, including `GlobalTimerResolutionRequests = 1`, rebooted once, preserved shell health, and returned `no-hit` for this specific candidate in the ETW-derived query surface. A later repo-native follow-up then closed the old trigger-design gap by adding `power-request-simulation` as a named guest Procmon profile plus a matching mega-trigger runtime alias, reusing the same `PowerCreateRequest` and `PowerSetRequest` primitive family that source-enrichment had already recommended. The next proof step is no longer trigger design or raw live state; it is a current-build reader or seeding path plus a narrow replay that explains whether the registry value is still an active override on modern builds.
